title: Six-State Primary Night Sent Both Parties a Mixed Midterm Message
thumbnailMessage: Primary voters rejected one simple national storyline
summary: Minnesota Democrats chose progressive Peggy Flanagan for Senate, Republicans rejected Trump-backed Mike Lindell for governor, and Wisconsin Democrats narrowly chose David Crowley—results that resist a single ideological label.
content:
Primary voters across six states reshaped the November ballot Tuesday, but the clearest national lesson is that they did not deliver one tidy ideological verdict. Progressives won a major open Senate nomination in Minnesota. The state’s Republican voters rejected a candidate endorsed by President Donald Trump in the governor’s race. Next door in Wisconsin, Democrats narrowly chose a more moderate candidate for an open governorship.

The results are among the leading national political stories on Aug. 12 because they test candidate strength, party coalitions and midterm messages in real elections rather than polls. They also require a basic caution: primary electorates are not the same as November electorates, and election-night returns remain unofficial until the states complete their canvasses.

Minnesota provided the sharpest contrasts. With all 4,105 precincts reporting early Wednesday, the secretary of state’s unofficial tally showed Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan winning the Democratic-Farmer-Labor primary for U.S. Senate with 411,456 votes, or 59.02 percent. U.S. Rep. Angie Craig received 274,582 votes, or 39.38 percent.

Flanagan’s victory was a clear win for the progressive wing of the party. The Associated Press described a contest in which she challenged corporate influence and attacked Craig’s vote for a Trump-backed immigration bill. Flanagan was supported by Sens. Bernie Sanders and Elizabeth Warren and by retiring Sen. Tina Smith, whose open seat the candidates are seeking. Craig conceded and urged her supporters to back Flanagan in November.

Republican Senate voters chose former sports broadcaster Michele Tafoya. The unofficial state results showed Tafoya with 211,631 votes, or 52.06 percent, ahead of Adam Schwarze at 23.96 percent and Royce White at 11.16 percent. The Minnesota Senate general election is therefore set between Flanagan and Tafoya, subject to certification and any lawful recount or contest.

The same Minnesota electorate produced a different message in the Republican primary for governor. State House Speaker Lisa Demuth and running mate Ryan Wilson received 179,546 votes, or 43.44 percent. Mike Lindell and Phillip Parrish received 134,198, or 32.47 percent, while Kendall Qualls and Brian Nicholson received 21.37 percent. AP and Reuters both noted that Trump had endorsed Lindell.

Demuth’s win is a reminder that a presidential endorsement is influential but not decisive. She campaigned on experience and electability and pointed to her role as speaker in a Minnesota House divided evenly between Republicans and Democrats. Some Republicans feared that Lindell’s profile and promotion of false claims about the 2020 election would weaken the ticket with independent and moderate voters.

Demuth will face Democratic Sen. Amy Klobuchar, who won the DFL governor primary with 614,354 votes, or 89.68 percent. Gov. Tim Walz is not seeking another term. The open governor’s race will test whether Republicans can end a two-decade drought in Minnesota statewide elections and whether Democrats can defend the state while addressing a major fraud scandal involving public social-service funds.

Wisconsin gave Democrats nearly the reverse ideological result. Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley narrowly defeated state Rep. Francesca Hong in the Democratic primary for governor after delayed Milwaukee absentee results were added. AP called the race for Crowley, while other national reporting placed the final margin at roughly 39.8 percent to 39.4 percent, a difference of just over 3,000 votes.

The delay itself is part of the accountability record. Milwaukee election officials said human error caused audit logs rather than ballot results to be uploaded to flash drives, delaying results for about 28,000 absentee ballots. A reporting mistake is not evidence that ballots were fabricated or altered. Officials should publish the incident report, chain-of-custody record, reconciliation totals and canvass result so voters can distinguish an operational error from unsupported claims of fraud.

Crowley entered the race as the more moderate candidate and received the late support of outgoing Gov. Tony Evers. Hong, a democratic socialist, built a strong progressive campaign and came within a fraction of a percentage point of winning. Crowley will face Republican U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany in November in an open race in a state that Trump carried narrowly in 2024. That contest is likely to draw heavy national spending.

Put Minnesota and Wisconsin together and the easy narratives break down. The same night produced a progressive Senate victory, a moderate gubernatorial victory and a Republican rejection of a Trump-backed candidate. Voters were choosing among different people for different offices under different state conditions. Treating every result as a national plebiscite erases what the ballots actually show.

The rest of the six-state map reinforced the theme of change. In Connecticut, former Hartford Mayor Luke Bronin defeated longtime Democratic Rep. John Larson in the 1st Congressional District primary. Larson first won the seat in 1998. AP counted him as the 10th House incumbent to lose a primary this cycle and the sixth defeated by a younger challenger.

South Carolina Republicans did not settle their special U.S. Senate nomination. Sen. Darline Graham, appointed after the death of her brother Lindsey Graham, and U.S. Rep. Ralph Norman advanced from a 10-candidate field to an Aug. 25 runoff. The winner will face Democratic nominee Annie Andrews. Because the runoff remains ahead, neither Republican should be described as the nominee today.

In Vermont, economist Amanda Janoo won the Democratic governor primary and will challenge Republican Gov. Phil Scott. In Alabama’s court-ordered redrawn congressional map, Trump-backed Rhett Marques won the Republican primary in the competitive 2nd District and Ammie Akin won the GOP primary in the 7th. Wisconsin’s 3rd District also produced a high-stakes November rematch between Democrat Rebecca Cooke and Republican Rep. Derrick Van Orden.

Candidate labels should be used carefully. “Progressive,” “moderate,” “establishment” and “Trump-backed” describe alliances and campaign positioning, but they do not replace a record. General-election voters should compare policy commitments, governing experience, financial disclosures, donor reports and fact-checked public statements. A primary victory is a nomination, not an exemption from scrutiny.

Turnout is another missing denominator in many election-night claims. Minnesota listed 3,889,533 registered voters at 7 a.m., but voters choose only one party’s primary ballot and the statewide races drew different totals. A candidate’s percentage of a party primary is not the percentage of all registered voters. Campaigns and commentators should report raw votes and the electorate being measured.

The official timeline matters too. Minnesota says state and federal results remain unofficial until the State Canvassing Board meets Aug. 18. Wisconsin and the other states have their own canvass and certification procedures. Media calls are evidence-based projections, not the legal act that certifies a nominee. Close races may also trigger recount rights defined by state law.

The parties now face concrete accountability tests. Minnesota Democrats must explain how Flanagan’s progressive agenda translates into statewide policy and how the ticket will respond to the social-services fraud scandal. Minnesota Republicans must show whether Demuth can unite Lindell and Qualls voters while appealing beyond the primary base. Wisconsin Democrats must demonstrate unity after a race decided by a few thousand votes. Wisconsin Republicans must defend Tiffany’s record in a toss-up state rather than relying only on national conditions.

National party committees will be tempted to reduce the night to fundraising copy. The more useful response is to publish their spending, endorsements and independent-expenditure plans race by race. Voters should know when an advertisement is paid for by a candidate, a party or an outside group and which donors financed it. The narrow Wisconsin margin makes transparent spending especially important.

The general election is Nov. 3. Between now and then, debates should force nominees to answer the questions the primaries exposed: immigration enforcement and civil liberties, fraud prevention and public-program oversight, affordability, health care, abortion, energy, war powers and loyalty to party leaders. Reporters should press for specifics and correct false claims regardless of which party benefits.

Tuesday’s results did not prove that America has moved uniformly left, right, toward insiders or toward insurgents. They proved something less dramatic and more useful: primary voters can reward ideology in one race, governing experience in another and generational change in a third. The midterm map changed, but it did not become simple.

RepWatchr’s standard for the next phase is straightforward. Use certified results when available, label the current numbers unofficial, publish turnout and spending, separate a presidential endorsement from voter choice and test every nominee against the same public-record questions. The winners earned a place on the November ballot. They have not yet earned the offices.
